ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Viral thymidine kinase (TK) is an enzyme encoded by α‑herpesviruses that phosphorylates acyclovir, enabling selective antiviral action. Understanding its role helps clinicians choose and monitor therapy for HSV, VZV, and related infections.

sections.p: Viral TK is a viral-encoded enzyme that converts acyclovir into its active monophosphate form, allowing selective inhibition of viral DNA polymerase. Diagnosis is inferred from clinical response to acyclovir and, when available, viral culture or PCR showing HSV/VZV.
b: Enzyme present only in infected cells
Requires viral TK for drug activation

sections.p: Severity is gauged by clinical presentation: uncomplicated mucocutaneous lesions, disseminated disease, or visceral involvement. Staging follows standard guidelines for HSV/VZV disease severity, guiding antiviral duration.
Primary cause is infection with HSV‑1, HSV‑2, or VZV. In immunocompromised hosts, reactivation or primary infection can lead to severe disease.
Typical presentations include painful vesicular eruptions, prodromal tingling, or disseminated rash. In severe cases, visceral involvement causes fever, malaise, and organ dysfunction.
Confirmatory tests include PCR or viral culture from lesion swabs. In severe disease, serology or PCR from blood may be needed.

t.b: Detects viral DNA; positive confirms HSV/VZV infection and guides therapy
Provides viral type and sensitivity; useful when PCR unavailable
Assesses recent infection; limited in acute setting

sections.p: Red flags include fever, systemic symptoms, visceral organ involvement, or immunosuppression. Complications may be encephalitis, pneumonitis, or disseminated disease.
Treat with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir, chosen for potency and patient factors. Monitor renal function and drug levels when possible. Avoid drugs that compete for renal excretion.
b: Valacyclovir – oral prodrug with better bioavailability
Famciclovir – alternative when renal function is impaired

sections.p: Assess clinical response after 5–7 days. Prevent recurrence with suppressive therapy in frequent recurrences or immunocompromised patients.
Herpes zoster can mimic shingles; HSV genital lesions may resemble other genital infections. Viral TK activity is not present in bacterial or fungal infections.
Low viral load may yield false‑negative PCR; renal impairment can falsely elevate drug levels. Clinical judgment remains paramount when lab results are equivocal.
b: PCR sensitivity decreases with low viral load

faq.q: Why does acyclovir only work in infected cells?
faq.a: Because it needs viral TK to be phosphorylated; uninfected cells lack this enzyme, so the drug remains inactive.

faq.q: Can I use acyclovir for any viral infection?
faq.a: No, it is effective mainly against HSV and VZV, which encode viral TK.

faq.q: What if the patient has kidney disease?
faq.a: Use dose adjustment or switch to famciclovir, which is less renally cleared.

exam: Explain the role of viral thymidine kinase in activating acyclovir and why this confers selectivity for infected cells.
Describe how you would manage a patient with disseminated HSV infection in a low‑resource setting.
Outline the key red flags that would prompt urgent referral for a patient with suspected VZV infection.
